questiontext.text: A binomial heap is best described as a...

answer.text: Forest (collection) of binomial trees, at most one of each order

feedback.text: Correct — the roots are linked in a root list, at most one tree per order.

answer.text: A single balanced binary search tree

feedback.text: No — it is a forest of heap-ordered binomial trees, not a BST.
That describes a binary heap, not a binomial heap.

answer.text: A doubly linked list of unordered keys

feedback.text: No — the trees are heap-ordered binomial trees.

generalfeedback.text: A binomial heap is a forest of heap-ordered binomial trees, with at most one tree of each order, so its shape mirrors the binary representation of n.

questiontext.text: How many nodes does a binomial tree Bk contain?

feedback.text: Correct — B_k has exactly 2^k nodes and height k.
No — the count is exponential in k, namely 2^k.
No — that is not the size of a binomial tree.
No — B_k has exactly 2^k nodes.

generalfeedback.text: B_k is formed by linking two B_(k-1) trees, so |B_k| = 2·|B_(k-1)| = 2^k, and it has height k.

questiontext.text: Merging (union of) two binomial heaps most resembles which operation?

answer.text: Binary addition of the two heaps' order sequences, carrying when two trees share an order

feedback.text: Correct — equal-order trees link into the next order, exactly like a carry in binary addition.

answer.text: Rebalancing rotations as in an AVL tree

feedback.text: No — binomial heaps do not use rotations.

answer.text: Rehashing all keys into a new table

feedback.text: No — merge links trees; there is no hashing.

answer.text: A full re-sort of every key

feedback.text: No — union just walks the two root lists in O(log n).

generalfeedback.text: Union walks the two root lists in increasing order; two trees of the same order link into one of the next order, exactly like carrying in binary addition, giving O(log n).

questiontext.text: What is the worst-case time of extract-min in a binomial heap of n elements?

feedback.text: Correct — find the min root, then union the children back into the heap, all O(log n).
No — the minimum can be any of up to log n roots, so it is O(log n).
No — extract-min is O(log n), not linear.
No — a single extract-min is O(log n).

generalfeedback.text: Extract-min scans the O(log n) roots to find the minimum, removes it, and unions its children (themselves a binomial heap) back in, all in O(log n).

questiontext.text: Inserting a single element into a binomial heap takes O(1) amortized time.

feedback.text: Correct — like incrementing a binary counter, insert is O(log n) worst case but O(1) amortized.
Insert is O(log n) worst case but O(1) amortized, analogous to a binary counter increment.

questiontext.text: A binomial heap with n elements contains a binomial tree of order k exactly when bit k is set in the binary representation of n.

feedback.text: Correct — the set of tree orders is precisely the set of 1-bits of n.
It is true — since B_k holds 2^k nodes, the present orders are exactly the 1-bits of n.

feedback.text: Correct.
